title: The Copilot+ PC branding is dead
content:
The Copilot+ PC brand is dead: Microsoft and PC makers quietly pull back on tarnished Windows 11 AI PC branding
In a new interview, Microsoft Surface CVP confirms that its new Surface PCs are no longer called Copilot+ PCs, but will still support all Copilot+ features.
In 2024, Microsoft and Qualcomm kicked off a new category of Windows hardware it called "Copilot+ PCs" that set the baseline for a new wave of AI-first computers, and launched with exclusive features that would not be made available on PCs that didn't meet a new set of system requirements.
The launch didn't go smoothly. Copilot+ PCs were met with immediate backlash from security researchers after discovering that Copilot+ PCs blockbuster feature, Recall, was woefully insecure. This forced the company to delay Recall and ship this new category of devices without its leading AI experience.
This pretty much tarnished the Copilot+ PC brand, and over the last two years more and more OEMs have dropped the moniker from marketing materials and product names. In fact, even Microsoft has seemingly stopped mentioning it.
I've noticed that none of the Surface PCs launched in 2026 include the Copilot+ PC moniker in their product names, unlike the Surface PCs that launched in 2025 and before. Now, you have to go digging to find any mention of Copilot+ compatibility in specification sheets.
At this year's Snapdragon Summit, I had the chance to ask Surface CVP Brett Ostrum about the lack of Copilot+ PC branding on its recent Surface PCs, and he confirmed that "these are not called Copilot+ PCs. They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there."
I've also asked Qualcomm's SVP of compute, Kedar Kondap, about his thoughts on the usage of the Copilot+ PC branding. He told me that "the purpose for Copilot+ PCs was to be able to deliver [NPU] experiences. So it was to define a certain category of devices with a certain bar and metric, like for example, a 45 TOPS NPU ... So from that perspective, it's more offering the same experiences, probably without just using [Copilot+ PC] terminology now."
It's also worth mentioning that NVIDIA hasn't gone anywhere near the Copilot+ PC brand for its upcoming RTX Spark platform, even though all RTX Spark PCs meet the Copilot+ PC specification bar. I suspect that's a deliberate decision.
It seems pretty obvious that the Copilot+ PC brand hasn't resonated with the market, and OEMs and Microsoft itself are now quietly pulling back on that branding. The specification baseline for Copilot+ PC experiences still exists, it just no longer has a pretty marketing name tied to it.
The rough launch of Copilot+ PCs, paired with the fact that Microsoft Copilot itself doesn't have a very strong reputation these days, likely contributed to the decision to slowly retire the Copilot+ PC branding. The brand never made sense to me anyway... these PCs have nothing to do with Copilot.

report.summary: Microsoft and PC makers are quietly retiring the Copilot+ PC brand while keeping the underlying AI PC hardware requirements and features.
report.background: In 2024, Microsoft and Qualcomm launched Copilot+ PCs as an AI-first Windows category with a 45 TOPS NPU baseline and exclusive features. The rollout stumbled when security researchers found Recall, its flagship feature, was insecure, forcing a delay and shipping devices without the main AI experience. The backlash tarnished the brand. Over two years, OEMs dropped the moniker from marketing and product names. Microsoft's 2026 Surface PCs omit Copilot+ branding, and executives now confirm the devices meet the old specification bar but are not called Copilot+ PCs. Qualcomm says the goal was defining NPU experiences, not the term itself.
key_points: Microsoft Surface CVP Brett Ostrum confirmed new Surface PCs are not called Copilot+ PCs, even though they meet the previous hardware bar. This shows Microsoft itself, not just OEMs, is stepping away from the branding while still supporting AI features.

OEMs and Microsoft have quietly removed Copilot+ branding from marketing and product names. The 2026 Surface lineup omits the moniker, and Copilot+ compatibility is now buried in specification sheets. The Recall security backlash and delayed launch damaged trust in the label.

Qualcomm SVP Kedar Kondap said Copilot+ was meant to define a 45 TOPS NPU device category, and those experiences can continue without the terminology. The hardware specification baseline remains, but the consumer-facing brand is being retired.

NVIDIA has avoided Copilot+ branding for its upcoming RTX Spark platform despite meeting the specification. This suggests the label lacks market value. Microsoft Copilot's weak reputation likely accelerated the decision to quietly retire the name.

The AI PC category continues through NPUs, local inference, and Windows AI features, but Copilot+ as a unified marketing badge is effectively dead. Hardware requirements and exclusive experiences may still be gated by specs, just without a prominent brand.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the retreat shows AI PC marketing is struggling to resonate. Vendors will likely differentiate through their own AI features, NPU performance, and software ecosystems instead of a Microsoft-led badge. Developers should still target the 45 TOPS NPU baseline and Windows AI APIs, but avoid assuming Copilot+ branding signals capability. Tools like ONNX Runtime, DirectML, and Qualcomm QNN remain relevant. For regular users, buying decisions get murkier: AI features may still require specific hardware, but the Copilot+ label will no longer reliably indicate them. Expect less hype and more focus on practical local AI, privacy, battery life, and real-world utility.
report.tools: To follow AI PC and NPU development, watch Qualcomm AI Hub, Windows AI Foundry, ONNX Runtime with QNN and DirectML execution providers, Intel OpenVINO, and AMD Ryzen AI software. For local LLM experimentation, try Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, and whisper.cpp. These open-source and vendor tools help test on-device AI experiences without relying on Copilot+ branding.
